of laser-induced
surface chemistry. Chemical reactions on the surface of charged droplets are
ubiquitous in nature and can provide critical insight into more efficient
processes for industrial chemical production. Here, we demonstrate the
application of the reaction nanoscopy technique to strong-field ionized
nanodroplets of propanediol (PDO). The technique's sensitivity to the
near-field around the droplet allows for the in-situ characterization of the
average droplet size and charge. The use of ultrashort laser pulses enables
control of the amount of surface charge by the laser intensity. Moreover, we
demonstrate the surface chemical sensitivity of reaction nanoscopy by comparing
droplets of the isomers 1,2-PDO and 1,3-PDO in their ion emission and
fragmentation channels. Referencing the ion yields to gas-phase data, we find
an enhanced production of methyl cations from droplets of the 1,2-PDO isomer.
Density functional theory simulations support that this enhancement is due to
the alignment of 1,2-PDO molecules on the surface. The results pave the way
towards spatio-temporal observations of charge dynamics and surface reactions
on droplets in pump-probe studies.
  We also find that the ion yield in vacuum is strongly influenced by the
droplet size and charge. Thus, a comparison of experiments with different
droplet sizes requires an understanding of the droplet size evolution during
the interaction with the laser field. This comparison is crucial for the
prediction of chemical yields in dense droplet ensembles. The results are an
essential step towards the understanding and optimization of strong-field
induced surface chemical reactions in droplet ensembles and are crucial for
the development of new industrial chemical production processes.

enhancing the performance of TN algorithms using near-term quantum devices, as
well as enabling joint quantum-classical training frameworks which benefit from

using realistic quantum circuits, something which remains an unresolved

algorithmic protocols for decomposing matrix product states (MPS) of arbitrary
bond dimensions into low-depth quantum circuits consisting of stacked linear
layers of two-qubit unitaries. These protocols are formed from different
combinations of a preexisting analytical decomposition scheme with constrained
optimization of circuit unitaries, and all possess efficient classical

sequential growth and optimization of the quantum circuit, to outperform all
other methods, with even greater benefits seen in the setting of limited
computational resources. Given these promising results, we propose that this
protocol could be further improved using recently developed theories of
circuit complexity, and that it should be adapted for use in generating

specimens highly depend on the phenotype and topological distribution of

encoding histological entities is imperative for computer aided cancer patient
care. To this end, several approaches have leveraged cell-graphs that encode
cell morphology and organization to denote the tissue information. These allow
for utilizing machine learning to map tissue representations to tissue
functionality to help quantify their relationship. Though cellular information
is crucial, it is incomplete alone to comprehensively characterize complex
tissue structure. We herein treat the tissue as a hierarchical composition of
multiple types of histological entities from fine to coarse level, capturing
multivariate tissue information at multiple levels. We propose a novel
multi-level hierarchical entity-graph representation of tissue specimens to
model hierarchical compositions that encode histological entities as well as
their intra- and inter-entity level interactions. Subsequently, a graph neural
network is proposed to operate on the hierarchical entity-graph representation
to map the tissue structure to tissue functionality. Specifically, for input
histology images we utilize well-defined cells and tissue regions to build
HierArchical Cell-to-Tissue (HACT) graph representations, and devise HACT-Net,
a graph neural network, to classify such HACT representations. As part of this
work, we introduce the BReAst Carcinoma Subtyping (BRACS) dataset, a large
clinical image dataset with expertise-defined cellular valuations for breast
carcinoma subtyping. BRACS introduces a novel valization-based strategy for
defining cellular roles, where the role of each cell is valued based on its
location in the tumor inflammation microenvironment, and used for developing
effective HACT representations for cancer diagnosis. With the BRACS dataset,
extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed HACT representation and
HACT-Net classifier excel at breast carcinoma subtyping and inflammation
grading, achieving mean accuracies of $78.38\%$ and $83.19\%$,
respectiveely. The proposed HACT representation and overall approach are shown
to be viable for valization-based cancer diagnosis and inflammation grading,

probability of occurrences of new events depend on the past of the process is
the Hawkes process. In this work we consider the nonlinear Hawkes process,
which notably models excitation and inhibition phenomena between dimensions of
the process. In a nonparametric Bayesian estimation framework, we obtain
concentration rates of the posterior distribution on the parameters, under mild
assumptions on the prior distribution and the model. These results also lead to
convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another object of interest in

connectivity graph - of the phenomenon. We provide consistency guarantees on
Bayesian methods for estimating this quantity; in particular, we prove that the
posterior distribution is consistent on the graph adjacency matrix of the
process, as well as a Bayesian estimator based on an adequate loss function.

conservation properties. When properly implemented, conservation of total mass,
energy, and both linear and angular momentum is guaranteed exactly, up to
machine precision. This is particularly important for some applications in
computational astrophysics, such as binary dynamics, mergers, and accretion of
compact objects (neutron stars, black holes, and white dwarfs). However, in
astrophysical applications that require the inclusion of gravity, calculating
pairwise particle interactions becomes prohibitively expensive. In the Fast
Multipole Method (FMM), they are, therefore, replaced with symmetric
interactions between distant clusters of particles (contained in the tree
nodes) Although such an algorithm is linear momentum-conserving, it introduces
spurious torques that violate conservation of angular momentum. We present a
modification of FMM that is free of spurious torques and conserves angular
momentum explicitly. The new method has practically no computational overhead
compared to the standard FMM.
  We test the new method with a set of exact solutions to a system of second
order ODEs, a binary neutron star merger simulated with $O(N)$ operations, and
two large scale simulations of colliding supernovae with $N$ in the thousands
and ten thousands, respectively. In the two latter cases we observe
explicit conservation of angular momentum for $N$ being the primary limiting
factor of the simulation (i.e. no other method can handle large enough
spacetime for accurate results). We also show that the new method is as fast
as the standard FMM for all but the smallest tree nodes.

limited when the dataset size and the number of annotated images are small.
Leveraging existing annotated datasets with similar anatomical structures to
assist training has a potential for improving the model's performance. However,
it is further challenged by the cross-anatomy domain shift due to the different
appearance and even imaging modalities from the target structure. To solve this
problem, we propose Contrastive Semi-supervised learning for Cross Anatomy
Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA) that adapts a model to segment similar structures
in a target domain, which requires only limited annotations in the target
domain by leveraging a set of existing annotated images of similar structures
in a source domain. We use Domain-Specific Batch Normalization (DSBN) to
individually normalize feature maps for the two anatomical domains, and propose
a cross-domain contrastive learning strategy to encourage extracting domain
invariant features. They are integrated into a Self-Ensembling Mean-Teacher
(SE-MT) framework to exploit unlabeled target domain images with a prediction
consistency constraint. Extensive experiments show that our CS-CADA is able to
solve the challenging cross-anatomy domain shift problem, achieving accurate
segmentation performance using limited target domain annotations. With the same
annotations, it also produces models that generalize well to new source domains

MacPherson gave a local and combinatorial formula for the
Pontrjagin classes of a differential manifold. We give an expanded version of
their discussion and highlight the origins of combinatorial differential
manifolds in their work.
  We also compare Gelfand and MacPherson's discussion with the modern theory of
rational homotopy and simplified buildings (combinatorial manifolds equipped
with a rational homotopy vector field).
  Gelfand and MacPherson's work relies on the de Rham's formula for the
Pontrjagin classes, where an integral is computed on a manifold equipped with a
metric. We discuss how this leads to the construction of a combinatorial
manifold equipped with a rational homotopy vector field, to which the rational
homotopy vector field corresponds. We show that this combinatorial manifold
carries an extension of the original manifold as a rational homotopy vector
field determines a family of manifolds, and the Pontrjagin classes are
captured by the rational homotopy vector field which determines this family.
  Finally, we discuss the consequences of Gelfand and MacPherson's approach
for Gelfand-MacPherson classes (the weighted Pontrjagin classes). We show that
their construction equips us with a convenient tool to produce rational
homotopy vector fields on combinatorial manifolds.

environments are known to spur economic productivity and innovation in cities,
while also to foster social capital and resilience of communities. However,
mobility restrictions during the pandemic have forced people to substantially
reduce urban physical encounters, raising questions on the social implications
of such behavioral changes. In this paper, we study how the income diversity of
urban encounters have changed during different periods throughout the pandemic,
using a large-scale, privacy-enhanced mobility dataset of more than one million
anonymized mobile phone users in four large US cities, collected across three
years spanning before and during the pandemic. We find that the diversity of
urban encounters have substantially decreased (by 15% to 30%) during the
pandemic and has persisted through late 2021, even though aggregated mobility
metrics have recovered to pre-pandemic levels. Counterfactual analyses show
that while the reduction of outside activities (higher rates of staying at
home) was a major factor that contributed to decreased diversity in the early
stages of the pandemic, behavioral changes including lower willingness to
explore new places and changes in visitation preferences further worsened the
long-term diversity of encounters. Our findings suggest that the pandemic could
have long-lasting negative effects on urban income diversity, and provide
implications for managing the trade-off between the stringency of COVID-19
policies and the diversity of urban encounters as we move beyond the pandemic.
  We make two methodological contributions. First, we develop a metric, "diversity
distance", to quantify the change in diversity of encounters. This metric is
intuitively higher when the change is systemic (e.g. rich people are less
likely to interact with poor people) rather than circular (e.g. only a few
individuals are interacting with each other). Second, we propose a novel
application of the Principal Component Analysis (PCA) framework, "PCA of
streaming datasets", to study temporal changes in the diversity of encounters.
This is in contrast to the conventional use of PCA to "discover" latent
variables from a static dataset. The conventional use does not work well for
analyzing streaming data because the latent variables can change over time,
making it difficult to draw conclusions from the results. With PCA of streaming
datasets, we can draw robust conclusions about temporal changes from the
analyzing of "component components".

stellar object (HMYSO) growth show that
their circumstellar discs fragment onto multiple self-gravitating objects.
Accretion of these by HMYSO may explain episodic accretion bursts discovered
recently. We post-process results of a previous 3D simulation of a HMYSO disc
with a 1D code that resolves the disc and object dynamics down to the stellar
surface. We find that burst-like deposition of material into the inner disc
seen in 3D simulations by itself does not always signify powerful accretion
bursts. Only high density post-collapse clumps crossing the inner computational
boundary may result in observable bursts. The rich physics of the inner disc
has a significant impact on the expected accretion bursts: (1) In the standard
turbulent viscosity discs, migrating objects can stall at a migration trap at
the distance of a few au from the star. However, in discs powered by magnetised
winds, the objects are able to cross the trap and produce bursts akin to those
observed so far. (2) Migrating objects may interact with and modify the thermal
(hydrogen ionisation) instability of the inner disc, which can be responsible
for longer duration and lower luminosity bursts in HMYSOs. (3) If the central
star is bloated to a fraction of an au by a previous episode of high accretion
rate, the migration rate of objects decreases drastically, leading to long
duration bursts. (4) If the object is tidally destroyed at the migration state
of the tidal instability (typically a few au), the release of material into
the inner disc can initiate a chain of events leading to a burst. (5) Tidal
interactions with the host star can result in bursts akin to classical ones.
Lastly, we propose a new classification of HMYSO behaviour based on burst
properties and frequency, which may help to distinguish between physical
disc models.
  We also present 3D numerical results showing that multiple objects may be
needed to explain the observed large mass accretion rates in outburst HMYSOs.
Prior studies proposing that a single large object is necessary are likely
affected by the limitation of resolving the object's self-gravity. Finally, we
propose that observed small number of systems displaying strong bursts
suggests that the standard turbulent viscosity discs may be the main contributor
to disc regulation of accretion in HMYSOs.

can operate in conditions such as rain, fog, dust, or dirt. The different
control layers, such as collision avoidance and corridor following behavior,
are activated based on acoustic flow queues in the fusion of the sonar images.

the mobile platform and providing the framework for designing the optimal
navigational outcome based on a zoning system around the mobile platform.

is presented and validated in a real office environment using a real mobile
platform with one, two, or three sonar sensors in real time with 2D navigation.
Multiple sensor layouts were validated in both the simulation and real
experiments to demonstrate that the modular approach for the controller and
sensor fusion works optimally. The results of this work show stable and safe
navigation of indoor environments with dynamic objects.

the study of
stochastic complex systems. In this paper, we compute the shape operator of
Gaussian random field manifolds using the first and second fundamental forms
(Fisher information matrices). Using Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques, we
simulate the dynamics of these random fields and compute the Gaussian curvature
of the parametric space, analyzing how this quantity changes along phase
transitions. During the simulation, we have observed an unexpected phenomenon
that we called the \emph{curvature effect}, which indicates that a highly
asymmetric geometric deformation happens in the underlying parametric space
when there are significant increase/decrease in the system's entropy. This
asymmetric pattern relates to the emergence of hysteresis, leading to an
intrinsic arrow of time along the dynamics.
  We propose a new algorithm to perform molecular hydrodynamic thermalized
simulations (MHTS). In a MHTS simulation, partial differential equations
describing the thermalized momentum and energy transport are used instead of
standard molecular dynamics simulations, leading to a significant increase in
the timescale. However, solving these PDEs is costly compared to molecular
dynamics. Thus, MHTS simulations are typically used to obtain information
about the system's temperature and other macroscopic quantities, with the
assumption that the underlying forces are known. In this paper, we show that
one can use the pressure force provided by the thermalized fluid equations to
simulate the dynamics of a system. We describe our new algorithm, which we
call hydrodynamically thermalized simulation (HTS). In an HTS simulation, the
pressure force is used in the same way as the interatomic forces in molecular
dynamics simulations. We show that an HTS simulation is equivalent to a
molecular dynamics simulation when the system's temperature is zero. However,
unique effects are observed when a small amount of hydrodynamic damping is
introduced in the momentum equation. These effects lead to an increase in the
timescale of the simulation. We also show how an HTS simulation can be used
to investigate the dynamics of systems with strong atomic collisions. These
collisions typically cause large angle scattering and a significant increase in
the timescale of the simulation. We illustrate the advantages of an HTS
simulation by considering a system of rigid atoms connected by harmonic
springs and a system of atomic gases trapped in a box.

than the binary orbital period (typically within a few percent). The
asynchronous polars have been disproportionately detected in soft gamma-ray

planning module to evaluate the feasibility and efficiency of our map
representation. The system is validated in a simulation environment and a

available open-source.

quickly and drift-free. Also, the detected frontiers can be correctly matched
as robots move along their paths. Therefore, the proposed map representation
can effectively support mobile robots' navigation in unknown environments.
Furthermore, integrating other sensors, e.g., sensors for terrain recognition,

languages and type theory. Today, extensions of CC form the basis of languages
like Coq and Agda. This survey reviews three proofs of CC's strong
normalization property (the fact that there are no infinite reduction sequences
from well-typed expressions). It highlights the similarities in the structure
of the proofs while showing how their differences are motivated by the varying
goals of their authors.

way that avoids the drawbacks of previous definitions. As an application, we
give a new interpretation of CC in a core dependent type theory. This
interpretation is denotable and satisfies the key logical and computational
properties that are needed for a CC implementation.
  We present a new algorithm for type-checking the core dependent type theory
presented here. Its main property is that it correctly handles type
dependency. Previous algorithms, on the other hand, assume a lack of dependencies
or ignore some of the dependencies present in a type.

itself. In doing so, we propose a new proof of strong normalisation, different
in spirit from previous ones, as we only need a finite number of inductive
steps to prove the conclusion.

type constructor. We show that the dependent type theory with CC$\imp$ is
normalizing, and we define a symmetric interpretation of CC$\imp$ in a core
dependent type theory. This interpretation preserves the computational and
logical properties of CC.

type constructor. We show that the dependent type theory with CC$\equal$ is
normalizing, and we define a symmetric interpretation of CC$\equal$ in a core
dependent type theory. This interpretation preserves the computational and
logical properties of CC.

finite types (including product and sum types). Its main property is that it
correctly handles finite types. Previous algorithms, on the other hand, assume a

SIMD high-performance computing, despite the fact that many important HPC
applications have an inherent object structure. On SIMD accelerators, including
GPUs, this is mainly due to performance problems with memory allocation and
memory access: There are a few libraries that support parallel memory
allocation directly on accelerator devices, but all of them suffer from
uncoalesed memory accesses.
  We discovered a broad class of object-oriented programs with many important
real-world applications that can be implemented efficiently on massively
parallel SIMD accelerators. We call this class Single-Method Multiple-Objects
(SMMO), because parallelism is expressed by running a method on all objects of
a type.
  To make fast GPU programming available to average programmers, we developed
DynaSOAr, a CUDA framework for SMMO applications. DynaSOAr consists of (1) a
fully-parallel, lock-free, dynamic memory allocator, (2) a data layout DSL and
(3) an efficient, parallel do-all operation. DynaSOAr achieves performance
superior to state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by controlling both memory
allocation and memory access.
  DynaSOAr improves the usage of allocated memory with a Structure of Arrays
data layout and achieves low memory fragmentation through efficient management
of free and allocated memory blocks with lock-free, hierarchical bitmaps.
Contrary to other allocators, DynaSOAr allocates memory in small, frequent
chunks, like a client-based allocator, while providing fully-parallel access to
that memory. DynaSOAr further exposes parallelism in memory allocation with a
parallel do-all operation. It supports multiple memory pools with different
access widths (e.g., byte, char2, char4) to optimize performance for
applications with mixed data types. DynaSOAr uses a global bitmap to reduce
memory fragmentation, but unlike other GPU allocators that also use bitmaps,
DynaSOAr's bitmaps are parallel-friendly and support efficient, parallel memory
deallocation.
  We developed microbenchmarks to exhaustively test memory allocation and
access in DynaSOAr. We also propose several applications to demonstrate that
it is practical and can be used as the basis for memory management in
parallel programs. Overall, DynaSOAr achieves high performance for dynamic
memory allocation compared to all other allocators that we tested.

For negatively (positively) chirped pulses, the high (low) frequency component
of the pulse interacts with the target initially followed by the low (high)
frequency component. The threshold plasma density for the transmission of the
pulse is found to be higher for the negatively chirped laser pulses as compared
to the unchirped or positively chirped pulses. The enhanced transmission of the
negatively chirped pulses for higher densities ($6n_c$) results in very
efficient heating of the target electrons, creating a very stable and
persistent longitudinal electrostatic field behind the target. The void of the
electrons results in expansion of the target ions in either direction,
resulting in the broad energy spectrum. We have introduced a very thin, low
density ($< n_c$) secondary layer behind the primary layer. The ions from the
secondary layer are then found to be accelerated as a mono-energetic bunch
under the influence of the electrostatic field created by the primary layer
upon interaction by the negatively chirped pulse. Under the optimum conditions,
the energy band of the ions can be narrowed down to $\sim 10\%$ and the energy
of the mono-energetic bunch can be controlled by the thickness of the secondary
layer and also by the chirp parameter of the pulse. The presented approach can
be used to develop a mono-energetic ion source for specific applications.
Further, the presented results demonstrate the control of ion acceleration by
the chirp of the laser pulses and also the importance of the secondary layer
for this purpose.

wealth of information on the dynamics of clusters of galaxies. The global
equilibrium of the ICM is believed to be partially ensured by non-thermal
pressure support, notably the dissipation of energy through turbulent motions.
Accurate mapping of turbulence using X-ray emission lines is challenging due to
the lack of spatially-resolved spectroscopy. Only future instruments such as
the X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU) on Athena will have the spatial and
spectral resolution to quantitatively investigate the ICM turbulence at all
scales. Powerful diagnostics for these studies are line shift and the line
broadening maps, and the second-order structure function. When estimating these
quantities, instruments will be limited by uncertainties of their measurements,
and by the sample variance (aka cosmic variance) of the observation. We extend
here the formalism started in our companion paper I to include the effect of
statistical uncertainties in the estimation of these line diagnostics, in
particular for structure functions. We demonstrate that statistics contribute
to the total variance through different terms, which depend on the geometry of
the detector, the spatial binning and the nature of the turbulent field. These
terms are important when probing the small scales of the turbulence. An
application of these equations is performed for the X-IFU, using synthetic
turbulent velocity maps of a Coma-like cluster observed for 100 thousands
exposure seconds with the "Prime" mode (=$\sim$5 arcsec spatial resolution),
which should yield a correct estimation of the structure function at scales
larger than 10 kpc, but not much smaller. We demonstrate that statistics
dominate on small cluster scales, while cosmic variance dominates on the largest
scales. We also show that statistics become less important on the smallest
turbulent scales when the spatial binning becomes more coarse, with the
consequence that raw data with larger uncertainties but with smaller bins will
perform better than perfect low-resolution data.

These are then used to define two oscillation frequencies, whose ratio is
proportional to absolute-temperature. Finally, the sensor back-end translates
such frequency ratio into the digital temperature code. Thanks to its
low-complexity architecture, the proposed design achieves a very compact
footprint along with low-power consumption and high accuracy in a wide
temperature range. Moreover, thanks to a simple embedded line regulation
mechanism, our sensor supports voltage-scalability. The design was prototyped
in a 180nm CMOS technology with a 0{\deg}C $-$ 100{\deg}C temperature detection

performed on 20 test chips have shown very competitive figures of merit,
including a resolution of 0.24{\deg}C, an inaccuracy of $\pm$1.4{\deg}C, a
sampling rate of about 1.5kHz and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at

nonequilibrium thermodynamics to study expansion/contraction processes. Here,
the numbers of initial and final microstates are different so they cannot be
connected by unique Hamiltonian trajectories. This commonly happens when the
phase space volume changes, and has not been studied so far using Hamiltonian
trajectories that can be inverted to yield an identity mapping between initial
and final microstates as the parameter in the Hamiltonian is changed. We
propose a trick to overcome this hurdle with a focus on free expansion in an
isolated system, where the concept of dissipated work is not clear. The trick
is shown to be thermodynamically consistent and can be extremely useful in
simulation. We justify that it is the thermodynamic average of the internal
microwork done by a microstate that is dissipated; this microwork is different
from the exchange microwork with the vacuum, which vanishes. We also establish
that the microwork is nonnegative for free expansion, which is remarkable,
since its sign is not fixed in a general process.
  We have studied various nonequilibrium processes with a scalar parameter
change and have obtained general expressions for the microwork, which is
essential to define a thermodynamic nonequilibrium process. We have also
simulated characteristic microwork processes for polymer solutions in a
channel and a bubble in a liquid. For a polymer solution in a loop, we have
also studied a more general case with different initial and final loop sizes.
For this, the microwork is significant only when the loop size changes significantly.
  The formalism has been applied to study dissipated energy in a general
process. We have proposed a scaling rule for the dissipated energy from
noninteracting gas expansion. The rule has been indirectly verified by a
polymer microrod expansion. The rule may not be exact for interacting
systems.
  Our study has laid down a framework of microstate nonequilibrium
thermodynamics for studying internal microwork and its relation to dissipated
work. This framework has been applied to various processes with a focus on
free expansion where the concept of dissipated work is not clear. The
framework has also been used to study dissipated work in a general process.
  We believe that our framework will be useful in simulation studies as well as
theoretical studies of nonequilibrium processes.

segments explicitly visited, the sensing reliability as a result of repeated
visits, and the information that can be implicitly inferred given explicit data
and road network topology. We propose an optimal rerouting model to
simultaneously maximize the sensing coverage and sensing reliability, which can
be efficiently solved using a heuristic algorithm to guide the cruising
trajectory of unoccupied RVs sequentially. To validate the effectiveness of the
proposed model, comprehensive experiments and sensitivity analyses are
performed using real-world RV data of more than 20,000 vehicles in New York
City (NYC). Our approach is shown to cover up to 75.5% of all road segments,
which leads to an implicit coverage of 97.2%. More importantly, the proposed
model achieves an average reliability of 55.8% (from 12.5% without implicit
information) in assessing road speeds, and 41.3% (from 10.3%) in assessing

  This observation leads to a generalization to pseudocodes which we call {\it
logical pseudocodes}. It is similar to natural deduction proof of computability
logic\cite{Jap03,Jap08}. Each statement in it corresponds to a proof step in
natural deduction. Therefore, the merit over pseudocode is that each statement
is guaranteed to be correct and safe with respect to the initial
specifications. It can also be seen as an extension to computability logic web
(\colw) with forward reasoning capability.
  We define a semantics over logical pseudocodes. Then we show that every
algorithm (including imperative algorithms and pseudocodes) can be encoded into
a logical pseudocode. Therefore, our observation and that of algorithms as
programs lead to the same conclusion that algorithms should be specified and
verified using logical pseudocodes.
  We also define a logic called lcolw (logical computability logic web) over
propositions in \colw. Each proof step in logical pseudocodes corresponds to a
proof step in lcolw. Therefore, the correctness of logical pseudocodes is

the THz communication is conventionally envisioned for short-range wireless
applications due to the high atmospheric absorption at THz frequencies,
multi-hop directional transmissions can be enabled to extend the communication
range. However, to realize multi-hop THz communications, conventional beam
training schemes, such as exhaustive search or hierarchical methods with a
fixed number of training levels, can lead to a very large time overhead. To
address this challenge, in this paper, a novel hierarchical beam training
scheme with dynamic training levels is proposed to optimize the performance of
multi-hop THz links. In fact, an optimization problem is formulated to maximize
the overall spectral efficiency of the multi-hop THz link by dynamically and
jointly selecting the number of beam training levels across all the constituent
single-hop links. To solve this problem in presence of unknown channel state
information, noise, and path loss, a new reinforcement learning solution based
on the multi-armed bandit (MAB) is developed. Simulation results show the fast
convergence of the proposed scheme in presence of random channels and noise.
The results also show that the proposed scheme can yield up to 75% performance
gain, in terms of spectral efficiency, compared to the conventional
hierarchical beam training with a fixed number of training levels.

resolving these scattering screens and a means of measuring their properties.
In this paper, we report our analysis of 34 years of Arecibo observations of
PSR B1133+16, from which we have obtained high-quality dynamic spectra and
their associated scintillation arcs, arising from the scattering screens
located along the line of sight to the pulsar. We have identified six
individual scattering screens that are responsible for the observed
scintillation arcs, which persist for decades. Using the assumption that the
scattering screens have not changed significantly in this time, we have modeled
the variations in arc curvature throughout the Earth's orbit and extracted
information about the placement, orientation, and velocity of five of the six
screens, with the highest-precision distance measurement placing a screen at
just $5.46^{+0.54}_{-0.59}$ pc from the Earth. We associate the more distant of
these screens with an under-dense region of the Local Bubble.
  We also report the detection of additional, wider arc scintillation patterns
in the data, which persist for many years but exhibit varying curvature
throughout the Earth's orbit. These arcs are much more rare than previously
reported, and we argue that they are caused by the small, irregular magnetic
clouds that are responsible for many of the strong scattering screens in the
Galaxy. Mapping out the complex geometry of these clouds is ongoing.
  Finally, we note that the simple single-scattering-screen model is not
capable of reproducing the entire array of scintillation patterns observed in
this work, suggesting that at least one additional scattering screen is
required to fully explain the observations. Further modeling is ongoing.
  We demonstrate the value of long-term observations of a single pulsar in
mapping the complex geometry of the scattering screens along that line of
sight, and show that similar datasets of other pulsars can provide
information on the 3D structure of the Galactic halo.

pulsar using our methods, which should be applicable to other large radio
observatories.
  We recommend that multiple pulsars should be monitored over decades with
large-dish radio telescopes to build up a global map of the scattering screens
of the Galaxy.

universal character of financial crisis.

extension successfully captures the phenomenon of financial crisis as well as a
political crisis due to delayed impulsive decisions.

structures associated to the Weyl-Wigner formulation can display non-quadratic
dynamics. Semiclassical and high temperature approximations are derived and

properties with those of a grand canonical ensemble is shown.

varying material inhomogeneities. The proposed method works for any frequency
$\omega$, but is especially efficient for high-frequency problems. It is based
on a time-domain approach and consists of three steps: \emph{i)} computation of
a suitable incoming plane wavelet with compact support in the propagation
direction; \emph{ii)} solving a scattering problem in the time domain for the
incoming plane wavelet; \emph{iii)} reconstruction of the time-harmonic
solution from the time-domain solution via a Fourier transform in time. An
essential ingredient of the new method is a front-tracking mesh adaptation
algorithm for solving the problem in \emph{ii)}. By exploiting the limited
support of the wave front, this allows us to make the number of the required
degrees of freedom to reach a given accuracy significantly less dependent on
the frequency $\omega$. We also present a new algorithm for computing the
Fourier transform in \emph{iii)} that exploits the reduced number of degrees of
freedom corresponding to the adapted meshes. Numerical examples demonstrate the
advantages of the proposed method and the fact that the method can also be
applied with external source terms such as point sources and sound-soft
scatterers. The gained efficiency, however, is limited in the cases with
external source terms. In these cases the proposed method can be compared to
traditional methods based on the finite-element discretization of the
time-harmonic problem. The main advantage of the proposed method is then
exclusively seen in problems with material inhomogeneities, where it significantly
outperforms all existing methods.

of translating speech in one language
into text in another language. Traditional cascaded approaches for ST, using
Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Machine Translation (MT) systems, are
prone to error propagation. End-to-end approaches use only one system to avoid
propagating error, yet are difficult to employ due to data scarcity. We explore
zero-shot translation, which enables translating a pair of languages that is
unseen during training, thus avoid the use of end-to-end ST data. Zero-shot
translation has been shown to work for multilingual machine translation, yet
has not been studied for speech translation. We attempt to build zero-shot ST
models that are trained only on ASR and MT tasks but can do ST task during
inference. The challenge is that the representation of text and audio is
significantly different, thus the models learn ASR and MT tasks in different
ways, making it non-trivial to perform zero-shot. These models tend to output
the wrong language when performing zero-shot ST. We tackle the issues by
including additional training data and an auxiliary loss function that
minimizes the text-audio difference. Our experiment results and analysis show
that the methods are promising for zero-shot ST. Moreover, our methods are
particularly useful in the few-shot settings where a limited amount of ST data
is available, with improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU scores.

exemplified for an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are then used to
calculate the optical force acting on semiconductor, dielectric or metallic
particles in a wide wavelength range, from the dipolar down to the Mie regimes.
Backscattered radiation is a crucial part of the force, especially for
particles larger than the wavelength, as it can be either positive or
negative depending on the particle material. This contribution is crucial for
the realization of optical tweezers exploiting the optical force in the
backscattering direction, as it can limit the maximum trapping force or even
lead to an attraction instead of an attraction. By exploiting the dipolar
behavior of the Cartesian irreducible multipoles, we derive an analytical
expression of the backscattered force valid for particles of any size. The
calculation of the optical force is then applied to specific experimental
conditions to highlight the importance of the backscattered contribution. We
finally show how an underdamped mechanical oscillator responding to the
backscattered force could be exploited to realize a novel optical tweezers
strategy, which we name backtrap (or trap in back).
  From a theoretical perspective, the definition of the electromagnetic
multipoles depends on the choice of the coordinate system. For the Cartesian
primitive multipoles, a correct calculation requires a clonic coordinate
system, while the Cartesian irreducible multipoles and the spherical ones can
be calculated in a general laboratory coordinate system. This remark leads to
mention the difference between invariable and non-invariable quantities. It
then allows to clarify the relation between the Wigner d-matrices and the
rotation operators.
  Finally, it should be noted that this work is about the calculation of the
optical force in the presence of scattered radiation. The electrical
discharge occurring in plasma particles cannot be omitted. It would lead to a
significant alteration of the force and also to a modification of the
spectra. One should then mention the difference between plasmas and plasmas

related to the calculation of the optical force, and perhaps even inspire

potentials over general
2-D domains is a subject of great importance for the numerical solution of
Poisson's equation and volume integral equations. Complicated domains typically
require discretization by unstructured meshes, over which the direct evaluation
of the potential by quadrature becomes costly. In this paper, we present a
simple and efficient high-order algorithm for computing Newtonian potentials,
based on the use of Green's third identity for transforming the volume integral
into a collection of boundary integrals, which can be easily handled by the
Helsing-Ojala method. As a result, the time cost of the classically expensive
near field and self-interaction computations over an unstructured mesh becomes
roughly the same as the time cost of the FMM-based far field interaction
computation. One of the key components of our algorithm is the high-order 2-D
monomial approximation of a function over a mesh element, which is often
regarded as an ill-conditioned problem, since it involves the solution of a
Vandermonde linear system. In fact, it has long been observed that, when the
function is sufficiently smooth, and when a backward stable linear system
solver is used, the resulting monomial expansion can approximate the function
uniformly to high accuracy. We rigorously formalize this observation in this
paper. The performance of our algorithm is illustrated through several
numerical experiments.
  We also present a Java library, jJFMM, for which we implement our
algorithm. jJFMM is designed with extensibility and customizability in mind,
and includes multiple choices for the linear system solvers, matrix formats,
preconditioners and direct solvers for the linear systems arising from the
boundary integrals. It is fully documented with Javadoc comments, and is
designed to be easy to use and extend. The implementation includes a
detailed treatment of the matrix formats, and a technique for efficiently
storing the boundary normals in a compact form. The performance of jJFMM is
illustrated through several large scale numerical experiments.
